articles.title: Stimulus category is associated with conscious access during motion-induced blindness
articles.content: Stimuli from different categories, such as faces or letters, differ in semantic content and neural representation. How stimulus category relates to conscious access during perceptual suppression has been studied mainly with binocular rivalry and continuous flash suppression, in which suppression arises from interocular competition. Motion-induced blindness (MIB) is a form of perceptual suppression without interocular competition, in which a static peripheral target intermittently disappears from visual awareness in the presence of a continuously moving background. Here, we tested whether target category affects the temporal dynamics of MIB using human faces, familiar Roman letters, and phase-randomized noise images as targets. Faces disappeared more frequently than noise and showed shorter invisible and visible episodes, whereas overall invisibility fraction and latency to first disappearance did not differ reliably. Letters showed a smaller increase in disappearance rate relative to noise, with no reliable difference in invisible episode duration. These findings reveal systematic category-related differences in the temporal organization of MIB and identify associations between stimulus category and the dynamics of conscious access.

articles.title: Show HN: Open-source early-reading reader with phonics help
articles.content:
My kid is 6 y/o and she is learning to read. She's moved through the basic phonics with Teach Your Monster to Read but was struggling with how repetitive it was. I wanted to give her some stories to read, but she still needed help sounding words out - and I wanted her to have the experience of sitting and reading by herself.

So I built this book reader app to allow her to click on the words, sound out the phonemes, and read by herself.

My 12 year old son wrote the first story, there's a cliffhanger at the end and he's working on the next section.

We're going to release more chapters and more stories in the near future.

And there's one other thing -

The reader has an MCP connection, so you can connect your Claude or ChatGPT or Grok, give them a PDF of a book you like (or even a set of scans done quickly with a phone camera) and have them import your favorite books into the app (private to your account, for your own kid, if you own the book of course).

The reader is free to use on its website and open source if you want to tinker and create your own version.

The included stories are under Creative Commons.

articles.title: A Relational Code for Objects in Primate Frontal Cortex
articles.content: When we remember a scene, we recall both the locations of individual objects and their spatial arrangement. Yet, how neurons encode this arrangement alongside individual locations is unknown. In this work, we recorded large-scale neural activity from the frontal and supplementary eye fields of monkeys performing a two-object spatial working-memory task. Using a continuum of two object configurations, we tested whether neurons encoded individual object locations or the spatial relationship between them. Many neurons had well-defined position tuning when a single object was presented. With two objects, responses spanned a continuum from retinotopic to relational tuning. Surprisingly, most units were better explained by relational tuning than retinotopic tuning. Relational and retinotopic units encoded complementary dimensions of the stimulus, and their observed mixture supported near-optimal population decoding of object locations. Relational tuning was systematically aligned with single-object receptive fields, enabling a readout that produced repulsive biases resembling those observed in behavior. Standard multi-object models such as averaging and normalization failed to reproduce the observed continuum, whereas a model integrating receptive fields over potential saccades captured it. These findings show that the frontal oculomotor cortex represents not only where objects are, but also how they are arranged with respect to one another.
articles.author: Watters, N., Gabel, J., Tenenbaum, J. B., Jazayeri, M.

articles.title: A new Mmrn1-CreERT2 Mouse Model for High-Fidelity Labeling of Adult Lymphatic Endothelium
articles.content: Cell type-specific Cre driver lines are essential for studying organ-specific biology in vivo, but recombination in unintended targets can limit their interpretive power. The dural meninges harbor a distinct network of lymphatic vessels implicated in neurological processes ranging from neurodevelopment to neurodegeneration. Current lymphatic reporters, driven by Prox1, Lyve1 or Vegfr3, efficiently recombine in lymphatic endothelial cells, including in the dura, but are also expressed in other CNS cell populations, resulting in non-lymphatic recombination that complicates interpretation. Here, we identify Mmrn1 as a gene specifically enriched in lymphatic endothelial cells throughout the body, with no detectable expression in other CNS cells. We generated an Mmrn1CreERT2 mouse line and show that, in adult mice, it drives recombination restricted to lymphatic endothelial cells, with no detectable recombination in non-lymphatic CNS populations. A similar but less complete recombination is observed in developing mice. This tool offers the lymphatic field a new means to specifically manipulate lymphatic vasculature and study its cell-specific functions.
articles.author: Goelz, C., Tavares, G. A., Lubera, J., Louveau, A.

articles.title: LATS2 modulates synaptic organization and function by regulating actin dynamics
articles.content: Recent work has highlighted the importance of core Hippo pathway kinases in cycling cells. Many of these kinases are also expressed in post-mitotic neurons, where they have been linked to synaptic function, and more recently a number have been shown to be dysregulated in neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimers disease. Despite this, little is known about the specific role or subcellular localization of the Large Tumor Suppressor kinases, LATS1 and LATS2, in postmitotic neurons. Previously, we demonstrated that LATS1 plays an important role in synapse development; however, the role of LATS2 remains poorly understood. Here, we examined the distribution and function of LATS2 and found that it is highly expressed in CA3/CA4 neurons of the hippocampus and localized throughout dendrites and dendritic spines. In contrast to LATS1, LATS2 expression remains stable throughout neuronal development. Furthermore, ectopic expression of LATS2 induces kinase-dependent structural spine defects, alters actin dynamics and reduces activity-dependent synaptic SEP-GluR1 fluorescence. Collectively, these findings reveal a unique distribution LATS2 in the hippocampus and demonstrate that LATS2 directly regulates actin dynamics and GluR1-containing AMPAR trafficking.
articles.author: Wigerius, M., Labana, P. K., Diab, A., Krueger, S. R., Fawcett, J. P.

articles.title: Cellular-resolution Three-photon Ultra-Deep Imaging (TrUDI) of neuronalpopulation activity at 2 mm depth in the mammalian brain
articles.content: Extending the depth reach of multi-photon microscopy for imaging neuronal population activity in the scattering mammalian brain is an exponentially hard problem. Three-photon (3p) microscopy has enabled imaging of neuroactivity at depths up to ~1.2 mm in the mouse brain. However, the fundamental depth limit of 3p imaging, as set by the depth at which the out-of-focus background fluorescence exceeds the in-focus fluorescence signal, is well beyond 2 mm. Reaching this fundamental depth limit in 3p imaging has been hampered by insufficient in-focus fluorescence signal arising from suboptimal optical design and acquisition conditions. Here, we demonstrate a Three-photon Ultra-Deep Imaging (TrUDI) system that approaches this fundamental depth limit via systematic and principled optimization of the in-focus fluorescence signal. TrUDI optimally matches the parameters of the excitation laser, the optical system, and the acquisition to linear and non-linear limits for safe laser exposure. At the same time, TrUDI remains compatible with the spatial and temporal requirements for single-cell resolution calcium imaging, and its parameters are tuned to the photo-physics of 3p excitation and the scattering properties of the mouse brain tissue. Our approach results in a ~250-fold increase in detected fluorescence photons at the same laser power as in previous approaches. We use TrUDI to demonstrate in vivo cellular-resolution recordings of neuronal population activity within fields of view of ~230 x 230 um2 at 8.6 Hz at tissue depths of up to ~2 mm in mouse cortex and hippocampus.

articles.title: Isoflurane anesthesia CNS recovery state: ultra-slow oscillations and cellular-stress-responsive gene expression
articles.content: General anesthesia and NREM sleep share slow-wave EEG features, yet whether anesthesia substitutes for physiological sleep remains unclear. We compared recovery from 4h of isoflurane anesthesia (IA) with time-matched sleep and sleep deprivation (SD) in male C57BL/6J mice using continuous EEG/EMG recordings and frontal cortex RNA sequencing. IA recovery produced transient, rebound arousal, reduced early NREM and REM sleep, and, fragmented subsequent NREM bouts, and persistant, ultra-slow EEG-oscillations that normalized within two weeks. Whereas, SD induced consolidated rebound sleep and slow wave activity. Transcriptomic profiling at ZT6 showed that IA and SD induced largely distinct cortical gene-expression programs. IA preferentially enriched integrated stress response and unfolded protein response genes, whereas SD showed a comparatively orthogonal, growth-permissive, mTOR-associated profile. Although IA-induced gene-expression suggests cellular stress, corticosterone measurements argued against systemic stress as the primary driver. These findings indicate that isoflurane recovery is neurophysiologically and molecularly distinct from restorative sleep.
articles.author: Dehnad, M., Bjorness, T., Kulkarni, A., Thai, T., Pandey, R., Loer, S. A., Konopka, G., Greene, R.

articles.title: Entering and Exiting Awareness are Asymmetrical: Evidence from tracking Continuous Flash Suppression
articles.content: This study provides a model for obtaining cleaner threshold estimates of entry into and exit from conscious awareness measured with the popular breaking continuous flash suppression (bCFS) and newer tracking CFS (tCFS) paradigms. In both, a suppressed target increases in contrast until it breaks into awareness. tCFS also measures exit thresholds by reversing the contrast change. Both CFS paradigms require a response when the threshold is reached and thus involve a reaction-time component. During this period, target contrast continues to change and threshold estimates are inflated (the "overshoot" problem). Here, we measure reaction-time components for both increasing (entering awareness) and decreasing targets (exiting awareness). We find overshoot is asymmetrical, being greater for stimuli entering (breakthrough thresholds) than for exiting awareness (suppression thresholds). To solve "the overshoot problem", we introduce a mathematical model that quantifies reaction-time components so they can be partialled out to produce clean breakthrough and suppression thresholds. The model can also be applied to previously published CFS studies. The model works for simple target detection and two-alternative target discrimination, even in the continuous tracking paradigm of tCFS. With the timing corrections applied, changes in pupil diameter around transitions in awareness are shown to align with the corrected time points, most clearly when targets exit awareness. Even after correction, the contrast decrease required for a target to exit awareness was greater than the increase required for it to enter awareness.
articles.author: Phan, C. K., Rideaux, R., Alais, D.

articles.title: Can We Really See the World in Three Dimensions? An Exploratory Study with Finger Alignment Task and Ponzo Illusion
articles.content: Stereopsis is the perception of depth when two 2-dimensional (2D) images of an object from slightly different angles align with corresponding retinal positions in both eyes. However, when we consider the blind spot (BS), a new set of challenges arises. In binocular vision, one eye's higher visual areas compensate for the other's non-receptive region. However, our brain only receives information from one image patch in the BS region, and another visual patch does not contribute to constructing a comprehensive 3-dimensional (3D) representation of the scene. This suggests that the brain adeptly manages this dimensional transition. We aimed to determine the extent to which we perceive 3D across our entire field of view (FoV). We employed the Ponzo illusion, a stimulus relying on visual depth cues (pictorial depth cues), and an eye-tracking technique to assess participants' accurate fixation and eye movement patterns. The participants attempted to align their index fingers before a chart paper to create a Horopter-like setup, supporting the hypothesis about our capacity for stereoscopic perception. The results of our exploratory pilot study with two specific tasks revealed that our ability to perceive depth diminishes beyond approximately 8$^{circ}$ of retinal eccentricity (in the horizontal meridian) in both halves of the visual field centered around the fovea. This limitation is not apparent in our day-to-day experience.
